label: text
content: - Let a and b be two sequences we want to compare, with $ |a| = n$ and $ |b|=m$

label: text
content: - We use a measure which considers both similarities (equal characters) and differences (substitutions, insertions, deletions)

label: text
content: Similarities: positive score

label: text
content: Differences: negative score

label: text
content: Recursive computation of alignment scores

label: paragraph_title

label: text
content: - We can actually simplify this when using a substitution matrix, denoted by $ \sigma$

label: text
content: Given an alphabet $ \Sigma$, the substitution matrix is a $ |\Sigma|x|x|\Sigma|x|\Sigma|-matrix$ which gives for every pair of symbols $ s_{i},s_{j}$

label: text
content: The matrix is symmetrical, i.e., $ \sigma (s_{i}, s_{j} = \sigma (s_{i}, s_{j}) = \sigma (s_{j})$

label: text

label: text

label: text

label: paragraph_title
content: Use of global sequence alignment

label: text
content: - Global sequence alignment is the "de facto" standard for comparing biological sequences that are directly related by evolution

label: text
content: Homologous genes or proteins between different species

label: text
content: ★ The "same" gene inherited from a common ancestor ("orthologous" genes)

label: text
content: ★ E.g., SHH in human and mouse; Pax6 in vertebrates and eyeless in flies

label: text
content: Homologous genes or proteins due to duplication events

label: text
content: * Genes derived by duplication from a single ancestral gene ("paralogous" genes)

label: text
content: ★ E.g., $ \alpha$-haemoglobin$ and $\beta$-haemoglobin$ and $\beta$-haemoglobin$ human (or in mouse)

label: vision_footnote
content: (from: https://www.differencebetween.com/difference-between-orthologous-and-paralogous-genes/)

label: text
content: How about analogous sequences (similar function but no evolutionary relationship)?

label: paragraph_title
content: Shortcoming of global sequence alignment

label: text
content: - Different types of macromolecules evolve at different speeds

label: text
content: Protein-coding genes (DNA) often evolve faster than the encoded proteins

label: text
content: ★ Redundancy of the genetic code (different codons can encode for the same amino acid)

label: text
content: ★ Chemically and structurally similar amino acids can often be substituted without effecting protein structure or function

label: text
content: Within a genome (and also within individual genes), some regions tend to be more conserved by evolution than others

label: text
content: * Genes are more conserved than the rest of the DNA

label: text
content: ★ Within genes, exons are more conserved than introns

label: text
content: * Within the coding regions of a gene (and within the protein it encodes) some regions are more conserved (e.g., functionally essential domains; negative selection against sequence alterations)

label: text
content: - Thus, in many cases, an evolutionary relationship can be identified only for a part of the sequences, but not globally, while for the rest of the sequences often no relevant similarity can be found

label: text
content: - We need a way of identifying similar regions within two sequences without requiring the full sequences to be aligned!

label: paragraph_title
content: Local sequence alignment

label: text
content: - Let $ a=a_{1} a_{1} a_{2}\dots a_{n}$ and $ b_{1} b_{2}\dots b_{m}$ is written as $ $ be two strings over alphabet $\Sigma$ for which we want to identify consecutive substrings which have a high degree of similarity

label: text
content: - Let $ \sigma\left(s_{i}, s_{j}\in \Sigma$

label: text
content: - Let $ w_{d} $ be a gap penalty (we consider only the linear model here; no distinction between opening and extending a gap)

label: text
content: - Let's continue to use our dynamic programming-based approach ...

label: paragraph_title
content: - Problem:

label: text
content: Find two substrings, one from a and one from b that produce the alignment (of the substrings! with the maximum possible score

label: text
content: or in other words:

label: text
content: Find the partial alignment (of substrings of a and b) with the maximum score (such that there are no other substrings which would achieve a higher alignment score)

label: text
content: - Of course we cannot know in advance how long the substrings need to be!

label: paragraph_title
content: Local sequence alignment

label: paragraph_title
content: - Problem:

label: paragraph_title
content: Find two substrings, one from a and one from b that produce the alignment (of the substrings! with the maximum possible score

label: text
content: - Observation: if the two sequences are not identical (e.g., if $ a \neq b)$ there must be operations with negative score (substitutions, insertions, deletions)

label: paragraph_title
content: - Two (rare) special cases:

label: text
content: - Since negative scores are possible, if there is no pair of substrings with an alignment score > 0, then the best solution is trivially given by two empty strings $ \varepsilon$ which have alignment score 0); trivial example: a="AAAAA" and $b=("GGGGG"

label: text
content: If we have no negative scores in the global alignment (only positive or zero) then the best solution would be the full global alignment

label: paragraph_title
content: - Complexity of the problem:

label: text
content: The two substrings with maximum alignment score need not be of the same length

label: text
content: Thus, we need a way to compare and align all possible substring pairs from a and b

label: text
content: We have $ O(n^{2})$ and $ O(m^{2})$ substrings, respectively

label: text
content: - Thus, naively enumerating all possible pairs of substrings would require to compute $ O(n^{2} m^{2} m^{2}$

label: paragraph_title
content: The "Smith-Waterman" algorithm

label: text
content: - Introduced in 198198198 by Smith and Waterman

label: text
content: - Designed explicitly for the comparison of biological sequences

label: text
content: - Guarantees to find the best (optimal) solution

label: text
content: - $ O(nm)$ instead of $O(n^{2} m^{2} m^{2}$! How?

label: text
content: - It's based again on the dynamic programming matrix!

label: text
content: Problem: how can we identify which possible subpath has the highest increase in score?

label: text
content: - Using global sequence alignment, cell $ (i,j)$ contains the total alignment score for the prefixes a(i) and $ b(j)$ , i.e., from the beginning, represented by cell (0,0)

label: text
content: - Idea: let cell $ (i,j)$ instead contain the maximum alignment score of all substring pairs which end at position $ i$ and $j$, respectively; that is, not from the beginning, but from some intermediate positions in a and $b$

label: paragraph_title
content: The "Smith-Waterman" algorithm

label: text
content: - We can achieve this by adding a simple 4th choice for each step:

label: display_formula
text
content: The additional choice is ... zero!

label: text
content: The motivation for this is the following:

label: text
content: - Computing a value for a cell (and keeping the corresponding traceback pointer) is equivalent to extending an alignment

label: text
content: But: if all possible extensions lead to a negative score, i.e., if $ M (i,j)$ would be < 0 then it's better to "reset" everything and start from 0 again

label: text
content: * Remember: we always can have a score of zero by aligning two empty strings, so any better solution must have a positive score!

label: text
content: - This implies: when the choice is 0 (resetting), no traceback pointer will be associated with the cell (no extension of a previous alignment!)

label: paragraph_title
content: Additional considerations

label: paragraph_title
content: - Multiple optimal solutions:

label: text
content: Highest score found in multiple cells; or, multiple paths from the same highest score We can:

label: text
content: ★ Report only one of them

label: text

label: paragraph_title
content: How about the second best local alignment(s)?

label: text
content: ★ Once we've found the best local alignment(s), we can iterate by finding the "second best score in cells which haven't been used for the best local alignment and trace back to find a second best local alignment ...

label: paragraph_title
content: We can iterate the previous point to find the third, fourth, ... best local alignment

label: text
content: * Remember that we can apply this algorithm to sequences of many hundreds or thousands of nucleotides/amino acids!

label: text
content: * In biological applications, we indeed often find multiple interesting local alignments between two sequences
